our_perspective: We think about premiums the way we think about energy: a recurring bill that design either reduces or ignores. At My Villa that logic sits inside the villa itself — a 250mm reinforced-concrete shell instead of a combustible frame, a Class A concrete roof, SFM-certified WUI vents at every opening, a non-combustible five-foot perimeter, and cross-ventilation modeled with Transsolar so comfort does not depend on machines running. None of it is decoration. Each item is a line an underwriter can verify, and each keeps working in the years when rates move for reasons no owner controls. We are accepting our first commissions now; for the moment, the specification is the argument.
body_html:
Home insurance has become one of the fastest-repricing line items in an American household budget. Yahoo Finance reports that average home insurance rates are up 47% nationwide, with increases that "far outpace inflation and wages" — and, in the detail worth pausing on, that Florida and California, long treated as ground zero for the crisis, did not appear among the ten states with the largest increases. Many of the states that did were selling affordable premiums only a few years ago.

Source: Yahoo Finance, "Home insurance rates are up 47% nationwide. See the states where rates rose the most."

What the numbers actually say

Two readings are possible, and only one of them is comforting. The comforting one is that California is no longer the outlier. The accurate one is that California started from a high base and is now surrounded by a national repricing that has nothing to do with any single fire season. When states with no wildfire exposure post steeper percentage increases than California, the driver is not local hazard — it is the cost of replacing a house, the cost of reinsurance behind the carrier, and a severity assumption that has been revised upward almost everywhere.

47% — national rise in home insurance rates (Yahoo Finance)

0 of 10 — steepest rate-increase states that were California or Florida (Yahoo Finance)

2 tiers — designation levels in the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standard

That shift explains why mitigation standards have moved from advisory to structural. The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety's Wildfire Prepared Home program is built on full-scale ember and radiant-heat testing, and it is organized around exactly the variables an adjuster measures after a loss: what the roof is made of, whether vents admit embers, what sits in the first five feet, what the exterior wall does when radiant heat arrives. It exists in two tiers, and the higher one presumes a non-combustible exterior rather than a treated one.

Source: IBHS, Wildfire Prepared Home

Why this matters in Los Angeles

For a client commissioning in Malibu, Beverly Hills or Bel Air, the practical consequence of a 47% national move is that the quote at closing is not the quote you keep. Location is fixed at purchase. Hazard mapping is set by the state. Reinsurance pricing is decided in Bermuda and Zurich. The single term in the equation that a buyer still controls — and controls only once, at design stage — is the expected severity of a loss in that specific building.

A premium is not a closing cost. It is a subscription that reprices annually, and the only variable an owner sets is the building itself.

This is why the interesting conversation in Los Angeles luxury residential work has quietly migrated from style to assembly. A stucco-clad wood frame and a reinforced-concrete wall can look nearly identical in a listing photograph and behave as entirely different risks in an underwriting file. One is a combustible structure with a protective coating; the other has no fuel in it. As carriers standardize around tested criteria rather than narrative descriptions of "fire-safe" finishes, that distinction stops being philosophical and starts appearing on the declarations page.

It also changes what good documentation looks like. The homes that price well are the ones whose drawings answer the questions before they are asked: roof class, vent certification, glazing performance, eave geometry, the material of the first five feet of ground. That is an architectural deliverable, not an insurance product.

What comes next

If a 47% national increase tells us anything, it is that premium relief will not arrive from geography or from a calmer year. It will come from evidence — buildings whose performance can be verified rather than described. For anyone designing in California in 2026, that argues for spending the design budget where the risk actually lives: in the structure, the openings and the ground plane, decided once and permanently.
